Nestling Fluttering shearwaters (Puffinus gavia) hatch from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], which is the temperature at which the incubated bird egg develops over an average incubation period of 50 days [ab = 50 days]. Upon hatching, these altricial chicks emerge at a wet weight at birth of approximately 40 grams [Wwb = approximately 40 grams], a figure representing the residual yolk mass and initial tissue of the newly emerged nestling. This modest starting mass is typical for procellariiform seabirds and reflects the substantial energetic investment in the yolk-dependent embryo prior to the first exogenous feeding. The chick then enters a period of rapid mass gain, sustained entirely by bi-parental provisioning. Field records indicate that during this phase, the downy chick is brooded frequently to maintain thermal stability, and parental provisioning rates increase markedly as the developing chick grows. This accelerated growth phase is critical for reaching the substantial asymptotic mass that characterizes this species later in the nestling period.

Under the sustained thermal conditions of approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], which is typical of the active metabolic period for a breeding adult bird, the nestling undergoes a predictable developmental trajectory culminating in fledging. The time since birth at fledging is reached after 79 days since birth [tx = 79 days since birth], at which point the chick has achieved sustained flight capability and its flight feather maturation is complete at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. The fledgling precursor reaches an ultimate wet weight of roughly 525 grams [Wwi = roughly 525 grams] prior to nest departure, a mass substantially above the mean adult mass of 330 grams. This elevated pre-fledging mass is a common strategy among procellariids, providing a lipid buffer during the critical post-fledging dispersal phase when the young individual must transition from parental-fed chick to nutritional independence. The attainment of this asymptotic mass represents the peak of somatic growth, after which the fledgling will gradually lose condition as it learns to forage independently. Studies of related species within the Procellariidae confirm that this pattern of mass overshoot is a consistent life-history feature.

The maximum reproductive rate of the Fluttering shearwater, when considered under conditions of optimal prey availability and adult body condition at the typical body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], is limited to a single egg per clutch annually. Females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and typically produce one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], which is the maximum clutch frequency observed for this species. This remarkably low fecundity is characteristic of many long-lived pelagic seabirds and is linked to the high energetic cost of producing a single, large, yolk-rich egg sufficient to sustain the yolk-dependent embryo through the prolonged incubation period. The investment in a single offspring per breeding season reflects a conservative life-history strategy where adult survival is prioritized over high annual reproductive output. Field studies across the breeding range of this species confirm that double-clutching has never been documented in this taxon, and interannual variation in productivity is driven primarily by attendance rates rather than clutch size.

Comparative data from related species, including the Manx shearwater Puffinus puffinus, provide context for the life-history parameters of Puffinus gavia. The maximum lifespan in the wild for this species is estimated at approximately 50.9 years [am = approximately 50.9 years], a value derived from long-term banding studies of congeneric taxa and recorded at a body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This exceptional longevity underscores a slow life-history pace, where the pre-reproductive juvenile and sub-adult stages are extended. The time since birth at puberty is reached after 237 days since birth [tp = 237 days since birth] under the thermal regime of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], indicating that sexual maturation is completed within the first year of life, although actual breeding does not commence for several more years. The gonad maturation and reproductive activation processes occur well before the first breeding event, a phenomenon common among procellariiform seabirds where young individuals prospect for colony sites and potential mates before attempting to reproduce. This post-pubertal delay is energetically advantageous in an unpredictable marine environment.

The age at first breeding for the Fluttering shearwater, based on demographic data from stable colonies, is estimated at approximately 5 years since birth [tR = approximately 5 years since birth] when recorded at the organism's typical active metabolic temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This delayed first reproduction event aligns with patterns observed in related Procellariidae, where young birds defer first breeding until they have acquired sufficient foraging experience and have secured a nest site and a mate. The extended pre-reproductive period, combined with the single-egg clutch, means that the lifetime reproductive output of an individual is constrained despite a potential lifespan spanning several decades. The maximum reproductive rate of one offspring per year, even across a lifespan of 50.9 years [am = 50.9 years], yields a low maximum intrinsic rate of increase characteristic of slow-living pelagic seabirds at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. Predation by introduced mammals at breeding colonies and changes in marine prey distribution pose ongoing threats to recruitment, but the life-history strategy of this species is well adapted to the stochasticity of its oceanic environment.
